test_title: PYST 73: RRB Group D - GS (Held On: 30 Dec, 2025 Shift 1)
subject: general
question: Applying pressure to a gas causes:
solution:
The correct answer is __**Particles to come closer**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• Applying pressure to a gas results in the reduction of the space between its constituent particles. Because gases have **large intermolecular spaces**, increasing external pressure forces these particles into a smaller total volume, which effectively makes the **particles come closer** to each other. ***Hence, statement 3 is correct.***
 
• According to **Boyle's Law**, at a **constant temperature**, the pressure of a given mass of an ideal gas is **inversely proportional** to its volume. This means that when pressure is increased, the **volume must decrease**, not increase. ***Hence, statement 1 is incorrect.***
 
• The speed at which particles move is a function of their **kinetic energy**, which is directly proportional to the **absolute temperature** of the gas. While increasing pressure through compression can sometimes increase temperature (and thus speed) in an adiabatic process, pressure itself is a measure of force per unit area and does not fundamentally define the speed of particles in the same way temperature does. ***Hence, statement 2 is incorrect.***
 
• When a gas is compressed (pressure is increased), work is done on the system. In most real-world scenarios, such as **adiabatic compression**, this causes the **temperature to increase** rather than decrease. A decrease in temperature usually requires the gas to expand or for heat to be removed from the system. ***Hence, statement 4 is incorrect.***
 
• The high **compressibility** of gases is one of their most significant physical properties, distinguishing them from **liquids and solids**, where particles are already very close together.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Boyle's Law:** Discovered by **Robert Boyle** in **1662**, it states that **P1V1 = P2V2**. This principle is fundamental in understanding how pneumatic systems and respiratory mechanisms function.
 
• **Kinetic Molecular Theory:** This theory explains that gas consists of a large number of **submicroscopic particles** (atoms or molecules), all of which are in constant, **random motion**. The distance between these particles is much larger than the size of the particles themselves.
 
• **Liquefaction of Gases:** By applying **high pressure** and **reducing temperature**, gases can be converted into liquids. This is the principle used in the production of **LPG (Liquefied Petroleum Gas)** and **Liquid Oxygen** used in hospitals.
 
• **Compressibility Factor:** In **thermodynamics**, the deviation of a real gas from ideal gas behavior is measured by the compressibility factor (**Z**). For an ideal gas, **Z = 1**, but for real gases, this value changes depending on the pressure and temperature.
 
• **Diffusion and Effusion:** Because particles in a gas are far apart and move rapidly, they can easily mix with other gases (**diffusion**) or escape through tiny openings (**effusion**). Increasing pressure can influence the rate at which these processes occur.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Industrial Applications:** Compressed gases like **CNG (Compressed Natural Gas)** are used as fuel in vehicles because large volumes of gas can be squeezed into **small cylinders** by applying high pressure.
 
• **Ideal Gas Equation:** The relationship between pressure, volume, and temperature is summarized by the equation **PV = nRT**, where **P** is pressure, **V** is volume, **n** is the number of moles, **R** is the **universal gas constant**, and **T** is the temperature.
 
• **Mean Free Path:** When pressure increases and particles come closer, the **mean free path** (the average distance a particle travels between collisions) **decreases**. This leads to an increase in the frequency of collisions against the walls of the container.
</ul
